Only one changes with the noun: [[ons]] for a [[het]] noun ([[ons huis]]), [[onze]] for a [[de]] noun or a plural ([[onze fiets]]). [[Je]] is the everyday "your", and [[jouw]] is for stressing it: [[jouw boek]], not [[mijn boek]].

contrasts.says: A noun's usual de or het tells you whether to choose onze or ons, even though you leave out de or het after those words.
Jouw means your before a noun, while jou means you as in ik zie jou.
English uses our with every noun, while Dutch chooses ons or onze to match the noun.

mistakes.why: Huis takes het, so use ons.
Plural nouns use onze.
Jouw means your before a noun.
Mijn replaces de here.

aan-het.explain: Put aan het before the full verb to show that an activity is in progress. The form of zijn changes with the word for who does it. English uses “am,” “is,” or “are” plus an -ing word, while Dutch keeps the full verb.
aan-het.why: To say something is happening right now, Dutch can say "I am at the cooking": [[ben]], then [[aan het]], then the full verb at the end. It's how Dutch stresses "in the middle of" where English uses -ing: [[Ik ben aan het koken]], I'm cooking. Without that stress, the present is enough: [[Ik kook]].

examples.text: Hij is een boek aan het lezen.
examples.literal: He is a book at the reading.

examples.text: Wat ben je aan het doen?
examples.literal: What are you at the doing?

contrasts.says: Dutch can also use ik kook for “I’m cooking”; ik ben aan het koken makes clear that the activity is happening at that moment.
Gaan can introduce a future plan, while zijn + aan het describes an activity already happening.

mistakes.why: Aan het takes the full verb koken.
This pattern needs both aan and het.

time-place.explain: The usual order is when first, how next, and where last. English often puts the time at the end. Dutch can do that too, but putting time before place is a useful starting point. You can move a part to the front to draw attention to it.
time-place.why: When a sentence says when, how and where, Dutch usually puts them in that order: time first, place last. English tends to put the time at the very end: I'm going to Utrecht by train tomorrow. Dutch says I go tomorrow with the train to Utrecht: [[Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht]].

examples.text: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht.
examples.means: I’m going to Utrecht by train tomorrow.
examples.literal: I go tomorrow with the train to Utrecht.

examples.text: We gaan vanavond met de bus naar huis.
examples.means: We’re going home by bus tonight.
examples.literal: We go tonight with the bus to home.

examples.text: Ze gaat elke dag op de fiets naar school.
examples.means: She goes to school by bike every day.
examples.literal: She goes every day on the bike to school.

examples.text: We gaan zaterdag samen naar de markt.
examples.means: We’re going to the market together on Saturday.
examples.literal: We go Saturday together to the market.

contrasts.says: When you move a time word to the front, the verb still comes second, before the word for who does it.

zijn-hebben.explain: Learn these forms together: ik ben/heb, jij bent/hebt, and hij/zij/het is/heeft. With wij, jullie, and zij meaning “they,” use zijn/hebben; with u, use bent and either hebt or heeft. When jij or je tells you who is or has something and follows the verb, use ben or heb: ben je moe? English also changes be and have, but its forms do not tell you the Dutch ones.
zijn-hebben.why: [[Zijn]] (to be) and [[hebben]] (to have) are the most used verbs, and they don't follow the usual endings: [[ik ben]], [[je bent]], [[hij is]], [[we zijn]]; [[ik heb]], [[je hebt]], [[hij heeft]], [[we hebben]]. In a question the verb comes first, and before [[je]] it drops its t: [[je bent]], but [[Ben je klaar]]? English be is just as irregular (am, is, are).

contrasts.says: The usual pattern with -t does not give you special forms such as ben, is, and heeft.
Dutch asks heb je tijd? by moving heb before je, while English usually adds do.

mistakes.why: Ik goes with ben.
Hij goes with heeft.
U keeps bent even after the verb.

demonstrative.explain: Use deze for “this/these” and die for “that/those” before a noun that takes de or is plural. With a noun that takes het and is not plural, use dit for “this” and dat for “that.” English changes these words for plurals, but Dutch also makes you check de or het.
demonstrative.why: Dutch picks its "this" and "that" by the noun's [[de]] or [[het]]. [[Deze]] and [[die]] go with [[de]] nouns and plurals, [[dit]] and [[dat]] with [[het]] nouns: [[deze fiets]], [[dit huis]], [[die boeken]]. English has one word each (this, that); Dutch has two.

examples.means: That book is a fun read.

contrasts.says: Plural nouns use de, so even a noun learned with het uses deze or die in the plural.
Ons and onze follow the same grouping: ons with het nouns that are not plural, and onze with de nouns or plurals.

mistakes.why: Huis takes het, so use dit.
Boeken is plural, so use die.

want.explain: Use en for “and,” maar for “but,” and want for “because.” When they join ordinary statements, the verb stays in the second spot in each part. A time word can take the first spot, as in want morgen werk ik. English “because” also translates omdat, but omdat sends the verb to the end.
want.why: [[En]] (and), [[maar]] (but) and [[want]] (because) join two whole sentences without changing either: each keeps its verb second. That's what makes [[want]] different from [[omdat]], which sends the verb to the end. [[Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben moe]] means the same as ... [[omdat ik moe ben]].

examples.text: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben moe.
examples.means: I'm staying home because I'm tired.
examples.literal: I stay home, because I am tired.

examples.text: Ik wil komen, maar ik heb geen tijd.
examples.means: I want to come, but I don't have time.
examples.literal: I want come, but I have no time.

examples.text: Ik ga naar bed, want morgen werk ik.
examples.means: I'm going to bed because I work tomorrow.
examples.literal: I go to bed, because tomorrow work I.

contrasts.says: Want keeps the usual order in want ik ben moe, while omdat sends the verb to the end in omdat ik moe ben.
The second-spot rule still applies after want, en, and maar, including when a time word comes first.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis, want ik moe ben.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben moe.
mistakes.why: Want keeps ben in the second spot after it.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ga naar bed, want morgen ik werk.
mistakes.right: Ik ga naar bed, want morgen werk ik.
mistakes.why: After morgen, the verb comes before ik.
